I'm 70 this year, and I've farmed these 20 mu in Quzhou for half a century. I studied at the agricultural college in Handan back in the 1980s, so I understand the science — NPK balances, yield response curves, disease cycles — but science doesn't pay the pumping bill, and at my age I can't lift what I used to. My son works construction in Shijiazhuang, so it's me and my wife most days, with our grandson helping on weekends when he's not in school. That constrains our labor severely.

I split the 20 mu into two parts: 12 mu in wheat-maize double cropping, and 8 mu in cotton. The cotton pays better per mu but needs hand-picking, and my back won't let me bend that much anymore. That's why I kept it to 8 mu — enough for good cash income, not so much that we need hired pickers for everything. The 12 mu in wheat-maize is our food security and stable base.

For the wheat already in the ground since last October: I planted Jinmai 47 at 12 kg/mu. I know from soil tests and 50 years of watching this land that 16 kg N/mu is my sweet spot — any more and the marginal return doesn't cover the urea cost at today's prices. I applied 8 kg N as base fertilizer before planting last autumn using compound fertilizer, and topdressed 8 kg N as urea at jointing in late March when the wheat turned slightly yellow. Right now, in late April, the wheat is at heading stage, and I irrigated just last week at grain-filling because April has been dry. That's the third irrigation for this wheat crop. I'm watching for powdery mildew — I sprayed preventatively with fungicide once already. I'm expecting 450 kg/mu if May doesn't bring a late drought like the one in 2014 that cut my yield by a third.

For summer maize after wheat harvest in early June: The turnaround is murderous — sometimes only six days between combine and planting. I hire the combine for wheat harvest, then immediately no-till plant Zhengdan 958 hybrid at 2.5 kg/mu using my small planter. I put down compound fertilizer at planting giving about 10 kg N, 5 kg P₂O₅, and 4 kg K₂O per mu as base. At the 8-leaf stage in early July, I'll side-dress another 6 kg N as urea. I can only afford two irrigations for maize — one at seedling if it's dry in mid-June, and one critical irrigation at tasseling/silking in late July. I'm targeting 480 kg/mu, though last year I got 520 because the July rains were generous. Maize is our most efficient crop per labor day.

For cotton, which I'm planting now in late April: I use Jimian hybrid seed at about 1.5 kg/mu. Cotton is a fertilizer guzzler and I know it, but our soil is moderately fertile from the wheat straw we return. I'm applying 15 kg N/mu total — split as 7 kg base at planting, 5 kg at first flowering in July, and 3 kg at boll-setting in August. I apply 5 kg P₂O₅ and 5 kg K₂O as base. I irrigate twice: once at flowering and once at peak boll. I spray for aphids and bollworms with insecticide — I've seen too many neighbors lose 30% yield to insects they ignored because the pesticide cost seemed too high. I also use herbicide for weed control. Yield target is 240 kg lint per mu, but realistically I'll be happy with 220 given my labor constraints during picking season.

On costs: My total cash outlay for inputs this year is about 10,800 yuan. That's most of my liquid reserve. I could push for higher yields with more fertilizer — my college training tells me 20 kg N/mu would maximize wheat yield mathematically — but my 50 years of experience tell me that keeping 2,000 yuan in my pocket for my wife's blood pressure medication and unexpected pumping costs is worth more than an extra 20 kg per mu. At 70, stability matters more than optimization. I don't have decades to recover from a bad bet.
